title: REBEKAH DIDN’T JUST GIVE A STRANGER WATER—SHE VOLUNTEERED TO WATER HIS CAMELS TOO
paragraphs: REBEKAH DIDN’T JUST GIVE A STRANGER WATER—SHE VOLUNTEERED TO WATER HIS CAMELS TOO

She thought she was doing an ordinary act of kindness for a thirsty traveler. She had no idea that a stranger's unanswered prayer, ten thirsty camels, and a divine appointment were about to change the course of her life. Sometimes the moment God uses to shape your future looks nothing like the breakthrough you've been praying for.
Nobody told Rebekah that her life was about to change.

There was no voice from heaven announcing her destiny. No angel standing beside the well. No crowd applauding her faithfulness. No dramatic sign telling her that this ordinary afternoon would become part of a story remembered for thousands of years.
Just a young woman carrying a water jar.
A stranger who needed a drink.
And ten camels that were probably very thirsty.
Rebekah gave the man what he asked for. Then she offered something he never dared to ask her for.
And the most extraordinary part?
She didn't know who he was.
She didn't know why he had come.
She didn't know what was waiting on the other side of her generosity.
She simply saw a need and decided that doing the bare minimum wasn't enough.
Before we go any further, ask yourself something uncomfortable.
When was the last time you did something good for someone who had absolutely nothing to offer you in return?
Not because they could recommend you for a promotion.
Not because they might remember your generosity someday.
Not because someone was watching.
Not because you could turn it into a testimony, a photograph, or a social media post.
But simply because another human being needed help.
That question takes us straight into Genesis 24.
And what happened there is far more profound than a charming story about a woman finding a husband.

Abraham was growing old. His wife Sarah had died. Isaac, the son God had promised, was still unmarried. Abraham sent his trusted servant to his relatives' homeland to find a wife for Isaac rather than take a wife for him from among the Canaanites.
The servant faced an enormous responsibility.
How could he recognize the right woman in a place filled with people he had never met?
He prayed.
Not for the most beautiful woman.
Not for the wealthiest family.
Not for someone with an impressive reputation.
He asked God for a particular demonstration of willing kindness.
Genesis 24:14 records his prayer:

"Let it come to pass, that the damsel to whom I shall say, Let down thy pitcher, I pray thee, that I may drink; and she shall say, Drink, and I will give thy camels drink also: let the same be she that thou hast appointed for thy servant Isaac."
That is the King James Version.
Notice what he was looking for.
A woman whose kindness would reach beyond the immediate request.
Someone who would notice more than the obvious need.
Someone willing to serve without knowing what she might gain.
Then Scripture says something breathtaking.
"Before he had done speaking, behold, Rebekah came out..." (Genesis 24:15, KJV).
Before he had finished praying.
Before he had even opened his eyes to search for the answer, so to speak, the narrative tells us that Rebekah was already approaching.
Think about that.
The servant was praying beside the spring.
Rebekah was walking toward it with her jar.
Neither knew the other.
Neither knew what the coming conversation would mean.
But the biblical narrator places those two movements together so we can recognize the providence of God unfolding through ordinary human actions.
Some of the most significant moments of your life may begin without announcing themselves as significant.
A conversation you almost avoided.
A person you nearly ignored.
A responsibility you nearly dismissed.
A small act of compassion that nobody else noticed.
But be careful here. Scripture does not promise that every act of kindness will lead to marriage, money, promotion, or a miraculous opportunity.
Kindness is not a transaction through which we purchase God's favor.
It is an expression of a heart learning to reflect His character.
And that distinction changes everything.
Because Rebekah did not know that the servant was looking for a wife for Isaac.
She was not performing kindness to secure a wealthy husband.
She had no reason to think a marriage proposal was waiting beside the well.
She simply responded to the need in front of her.
Genesis 24:17–20 tells us:
"And the servant ran to meet her, and said, Let me, I pray thee, drink a little water of thy pitcher.
And she said, Drink, my lord: and she hasted, and let down her pitcher upon her hand, and gave him drink.
And when she had done giving him drink, she said, I will draw water for thy camels also, until they have done drinking.
And she hasted, and emptied her pitcher into the trough, and ran again unto the well to draw water, and drew for all his camels."
Read that last sentence again.
She ran again.
And she drew water for all his camels.
Not one.
Not two.
Ten.
The number comes from Genesis 24:10, where the servant takes ten of his master's camels.
Now imagine the scene.
The weight of the jar.
The repeated trips.
The water being poured into the trough.
The physical effort of drawing more.
The sun, the dust, the interruption to whatever plans she had for the evening.

The text does not tell us exactly how much water the camels drank, how long the work took, or how deep the well was. Camels can drink substantial amounts of water, but we should not invent a precise number of gallons or claim Scripture gives us an exact workload.
What Scripture does tell us is enough.
Rebekah offered to keep drawing water until the animals had finished drinking.
She was willing to complete what she volunteered to do.
And that is where this story begins reaching into places we would rather keep hidden.
Because many of us love the idea of kindness until kindness becomes inconvenient.
We want to be generous, provided generosity does not interrupt our schedule.
We want to be compassionate, provided compassion does not cost us too much.
We want to be servants of God, provided service does not make us uncomfortable.
We pray, "Lord, use me."
Then someone needs our patience, and we become irritated.
Someone needs our forgiveness, and we rehearse their offense.
Someone needs our time, and we begin calculating what we will lose.
Someone needs practical help, and we quietly hope another person will volunteer.
And suddenly, the question is no longer whether we admire Rebekah.
The question is whether we recognize ourselves.
Perhaps you have been asking God to give you a greater purpose while overlooking the ordinary responsibilities already in your hands.
Perhaps you have been praying for a door to open while growing resentful of the people God has called you to love.
Perhaps you have been waiting for a spectacular assignment when faithfulness is being tested in the quiet places nobody applauds.
Or perhaps the opposite is true.
Perhaps you have been giving and giving until your heart feels empty.
You have cared for everyone else.
You have carried burdens nobody noticed.
You have served faithfully while people assumed you would always be available.
And now a story about a woman watering ten camels sounds less like inspiration and more like another demand placed on your exhausted shoulders.
If that is you, please hear this carefully.
Rebekah's generosity is not permission for other people to exploit your kindness.
The Bible does not command you to destroy your health, abandon necessary boundaries, or remain in abusive situations to prove your faith.
Jesus Himself withdrew from crowds to pray (Luke 5:16). He taught His disciples to rest (Mark 6:31). And when He called His followers to love, He never taught that love requires enabling wrongdoing.
The beauty of Rebekah's action is that she volunteered freely.
She was not threatened.
She was not manipulated by a promise of reward.
The servant asked for a drink for himself. She chose to offer water for the animals.
Her generosity was willing.
And Scripture draws our attention to that willingness.
There is a beautiful detail in the original Hebrew that deserves our attention.
In Genesis 24:18, the word translated "she hasted" is וַתְּמַהֵר (vattemaher), from the Hebrew root מהר (m-h-r), meaning to hurry or act quickly.
In verse 20, that same form appears again.
The narrative also uses וַתָּרָץ (vattarots), from the root רוץ (r-w-ts), meaning "she ran."
The repeated language creates movement.
She hurried.
She lowered the jar.
She gave him a drink.
She hurried again.
She emptied the jar.
She ran back to the well.
She drew more water.
The text does not merely tell us that Rebekah was kind. It shows us her kindness through her actions.
There is no indication that she stopped to negotiate a reward.
No evidence that she asked the servant whether he could afford to compensate her.
No suggestion that she knew the identity of the family he represented.
Her actions moved ahead of any expectation of payment.
And then Genesis 24:21 gives us another remarkable detail:
"And the man wondering at her held his peace, to wit whether the LORD had made his journey prosperous or not." (KJV)
He watched her in silence.
Imagine that.
The man who had just prayed was now observing the very response he had asked God to provide.
But notice the careful wording.
He was still discerning whether the LORD had prospered his journey.
He did not immediately declare the matter settled.
He watched.
Later, he asked about her family. He learned that she belonged to Abraham's extended family. He worshiped God, recounted the events, and sought the family's response.
Genesis 24 does not encourage reckless decisions based on a single coincidence.
It portrays prayer, providence, observation, conversation, family involvement, and ultimately Rebekah's own willingness to go.
When her family asked whether she would leave with the servant, Genesis 24:58 records her answer:
"I will go."
Two simple words.
But what courage they carried.
She agreed to leave her home and travel toward a future she had not yet seen.
The woman who had willingly served a stranger at the well was now willing to step into an unfamiliar chapter of life.
Yet we must not romanticize the whole story as though her future became a trouble-free fairy tale.
It didn't.
Rebekah would eventually experience the pain of barrenness before conceiving (Genesis 25:21).
She would carry twins whose conflict began even before birth.
She would become entangled in family favoritism and deception.
Genesis 27 records her involvement in a plan for Jacob to deceive Isaac and receive the blessing intended for Esau.
The same woman whose generosity shines so beautifully in Genesis 24 would later make morally troubling choices.
And this is where the story becomes even more personal.
Because the Bible does not give us Rebekah as a flawless heroine.
It gives us a real woman.
Capable of remarkable kindness.
Capable of courageous faith.
And capable of serious failure.
Does that sound familiar?
Maybe you have moments in your life when you can genuinely see God's grace at work.
You have helped someone without expecting anything.
You have prayed when everything looked hopeless.
You have obeyed even when you were afraid.
But you also remember the things you wish you could undo.
The words spoken in anger.
The relationships damaged by pride.
The compromises nobody knows about.
The decisions you made because you were terrified of losing control.
The moments when you trusted your own schemes more than God's promises.
And somewhere deep inside, a painful question keeps returning.
Can God still work through someone like me?
Look carefully at the biblical story.
God's covenant purposes continued through Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, even though the people involved were deeply imperfect.
That does not mean God approved of every decision they made.
It means human failure did not overthrow His faithfulness.
And that is the doorway through which we begin to see something greater than Rebekah.
We begin to see our need for Jesus Christ.
Because Rebekah's generosity is admirable.
But generosity cannot erase sin.
Her willingness to serve is beautiful.
But service cannot make a sinner righteous before a holy God.
Even the finest moments of human goodness cannot become a substitute for the saving work of Christ.
We need more than an inspiring example.
We need a Savior.
And the Gospel tells us that God has provided One.
The New Testament says in Romans 5:8:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had repaired everything.
Not after we had proven our worth.
Not after we had become generous enough, disciplined enough, religious enough, or morally impressive enough.
While we were sinners.
Christ died for us.
The Greek expression in that verse, ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν (eti hamartōlōn ontōn hēmōn), communicates that we were still sinners when Christ demonstrated His love through His death.
That is not a minor theological detail.
It is the difference between Christianity and every attempt to save ourselves through our own performance.
Rebekah offered water to a stranger.
Jesus offered Himself for sinners.
Rebekah's act met an immediate physical need.
Jesus, through His death and resurrection, provides the only sufficient foundation for forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life.
We should not pretend that Genesis 24 explicitly identifies Rebekah's water as a prophecy of Jesus. It does not.
But as we read the whole Bible, we can recognize a meaningful contrast between human kindness and the infinitely greater grace revealed in Christ.
And there is another encounter involving water that brings the Gospel into even sharper focus.
In John 4, Jesus sat beside a well in Samaria.
A woman came to draw water.
Jesus asked her for a drink.
That detail alone is striking.
The Son of God, who created the heavens and the earth, entered the limitations of genuine human life and experienced thirst.
But the conversation soon moved beyond physical water.
Jesus told her:
"Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again:
But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst..." (John 4:13–14, KJV)
The woman at the well had a complicated personal history.
Jesus knew it.
He did not need her to pretend.
He did not flatter her sin.
He exposed the truth while opening the way to something she desperately needed.
Living water.
A life transformed by the grace and truth of God.
And when the encounter was over, she went back to her community and told people about Jesus.
A woman who came to draw ordinary water became a witness to the One who gives living water.
Do you see the beauty?
At one well in Genesis, a woman freely gave water to a stranger.
At another well in John, the Savior offered living water to a woman who needed Him.
Different encounters.
Different purposes in Scripture.
But together they confront us with a question that reaches beyond the surface of our religious activity.
Have you spent your whole life trying to prove that you are good enough, while neglecting the living water only Jesus can give?
Maybe you are exhausted because you have made usefulness your identity.
You believe you are valuable only when you are helping.
Only when you are producing.
Only when you are sacrificing.
Only when people need you.
You have learned to say yes while your heart is quietly breaking.
You have become the dependable one.
The strong one.
The one who never complains.
The one everyone calls when something goes wrong.
But who listens when you are the one falling apart?
Who notices when your smile is covering grief?
Who knows how many nights you have cried after spending the entire day encouraging everyone else?
Please understand this.
Jesus did not die so that you could spend your life desperately earning the right to be loved.
He loved us first.
First John 4:19 says:
"We love him, because he first loved us." (KJV)
Christian service is meant to grow out of grace, not become a desperate attempt to purchase it.
Ephesians 2:8–10 makes the order unmistakable.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works. Yet we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace comes first.
Then a transformed life bears fruit.
We do not serve to become worthy of Christ's love.
We serve because His love has reached us.
And that is what makes the ordinary moments of life so sacred.
The meal prepared for someone who cannot repay you.
The patient conversation with a struggling child.
The honest apology you have been avoiding.
The quiet generosity offered without public recognition.
The decision to pray for someone instead of spreading another rumor.
The courage to tell the truth when lying would protect your image.
The choice to help someone without turning their need into an opportunity to make yourself look spiritual.
None of these acts purchases salvation.
But each can become an expression of the new life Christ is forming in His people.
Jesus said in Matthew 5:16:
"Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven." (KJV)
Notice where the glory belongs.
Not to the servant.
Not to the person who receives applause.
Not to the ministry.
Not to the one who gives the largest donation.
To the Father in heaven.
That is the kind of service the Gospel produces.
Service that points beyond itself.
And perhaps this is why the story of Rebekah at the well is so unforgettable.
She did not know that generations would read about her.
She did not know that her actions would be preserved in Scripture.
She simply did the next good thing in front of her.
But her story also warns us against a subtle temptation.
We can turn generosity into another form of self-interest.
We can begin to think, "If I water enough camels, God will finally give me my Isaac."
If I serve more, He will give me the relationship.
If I donate more, He will increase my income.
If I sacrifice more, He will remove my suffering.
If I do enough for the church, He will owe me the breakthrough I have been waiting for.
But God is not a debtor to human generosity.
And Genesis 24 is not a formula for forcing His hand.
Rebekah did not earn Isaac through a calculated act of service.
The narrative presents her kindness as part of the servant's prayerful recognition of God's providence.
The lesson is not that every good deed guarantees an earthly reward.
The lesson is that faithfulness matters even when we cannot see what God is doing.
Sometimes you will help someone, and nobody will thank you.
Sometimes you will forgive, and the relationship will not be restored.
Sometimes you will obey God, and your circumstances will become harder before they become easier.
Sometimes you will pray, and the answer will not arrive in the way you imagined.
But the worth of obedience is not measured by the speed of its reward.
It is measured by the worthiness of the Lord we obey.
Galatians 6:9 encourages believers:
"And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not." (KJV)
That promise calls us to perseverance. It should not be reduced to a guarantee of wealth, romance, or immediate success.
Our hope is greater than any of those things.
Our hope is Christ Himself.
And maybe that is what someone reading this needs to remember today.
You are not forgotten because your kindness went unnoticed.
You are not abandoned because your prayers have taken longer than you expected.
You are not spiritually worthless because your life looks ordinary.
And you are not beyond redemption because you have made mistakes that still bring tears to your eyes.
The same Bible that records Rebekah's generosity also records the failures of God's covenant family.
The same Scriptures that show us the beauty of faithful service ultimately lead us to the crucified and risen Christ.
A Savior who did not merely tell us to love.
He loved.
A Savior who did not merely command sacrifice.
He gave Himself.
A Savior who did not merely speak about forgiveness.
He bore our sins.
First Peter 2:24 says that Christ "his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree."
And because He rose from the dead, forgiveness is not an empty religious wish.
It is the gift of the living Savior to those who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that good people eventually become impressive enough for God to accept them.
But that sinners can be forgiven, reconciled, and transformed through Jesus Christ.
From shame to mercy.
From rebellion to repentance.
From spiritual death to new life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the past never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by erasing the consequences of every choice.
But by offering real forgiveness, a new standing before God, and the transforming power of His Spirit.
And now I want to speak to the person who almost stopped reading.
The person who feels like there is nothing extraordinary left in their life.
You wake up.
You work.
You care for people.
You pay bills.
You carry responsibilities.
You fight temptations.
You try to pray.
You try to stay faithful.
And some days, you wonder whether any of it matters.
Remember the well.
Remember the water jar.
Remember the ten camels.
Remember the woman who did not know that her ordinary afternoon would become part of a much larger story.
Then remember something even greater.
Your worth is not determined by whether your story becomes famous.
Your worth is not measured by how many people applaud your sacrifices.
And your eternal hope is not found in the possibility that your next act of kindness will unlock a spectacular blessing.
Your hope is in Jesus Christ.
The One who sees what others overlook.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who receives those who come to Him in faith.
The One who can change the direction of a life that seems hopelessly lost.
If you have wandered from Him, come home.
If you have been hiding sin, bring it into His light.
If you have been trusting your own goodness to save you, lay down that impossible burden.
If you have been serving until your soul is exhausted, remember that Christ calls His people not only to work, but also to abide in Him.
And if you have never truly surrendered your life to Jesus, do not confuse admiration for Christian values with saving faith in Christ.
Turn to Him.
Confess your sin.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Receive His grace.
Follow Him.
Not because you can repay what He has done.
But because His mercy is greater than anything you could ever earn.
And if this message has touched a part of your life that you rarely speak about, I want to invite you to do something more meaningful than leaving a routine religious comment.
Be honest.

You do not have to share private details or publicly confess things that should be handled with trusted pastoral care. But perhaps your words will remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
Someone else may need to hear that grace still reaches people in the middle of their unfinished stories.
Before you leave, think of one person who needs this message.
Not the person you want to criticize.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Someone you genuinely love.
Someone who has been doing their best while quietly falling apart.
Someone who thinks God has forgotten them.
Someone who has confused endless religious activity with intimacy with Christ.
Someone who needs to hear that the Gospel is not a demand to earn love but an invitation to receive the mercy of Jesus and walk in new obedience.
One thoughtful share can place Scripture in front of someone who might never intentionally search for a Christian message.
Return to it when your service becomes mechanical.
When resentment begins growing.
When you are tempted to measure God's love by the rewards you receive.
When you need to remember that ordinary faithfulness matters, but only Christ can save.
And if you are not yet following Gospel Warrior, I invite you to stay connected.
Invite your family, your friends, your fellow believers, and even the people who are still searching for answers about Jesus.

We want this community to be a place where biblical truth is not watered down, wounded hearts are treated with compassion, repentance is taken seriously, and the grace of Jesus Christ remains at the center.
Because spiritual growth is not meant to happen through occasional emotional inspiration alone.
We need Scripture.
We need sound teaching.
We need prayer.
We need encouragement.
We need correction when we are drifting.
And we need to keep returning to the Gospel when the noise of life begins drowning out the truth.
That is also why I want to extend a personal invitation to those who believe in the mission of Gospel Warrior and want to help it continue.
Not because God measures your faith by whether you support a particular ministry.
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ, never a product for sale.
Philippians 1:5 speaks of believers' "fellowship in the gospel."
And 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not promises of financial miracles.
But willing partnership.
These products are simply resources and reminders that can encourage faith and conversation. They are not the reason we preach Christ.
Jesus is.
The library is part of our desire to make biblical encouragement and spiritual nourishment accessible, not merely to those who can pay, but also to those who cannot.
We would be grateful to have you walking alongside this ministry as we continue pointing people to repentance, forgiveness, healing, and transformation through Jesus Christ.
It is to come to Jesus.
Because the greatest need of your soul cannot be satisfied by a ministry, a product, an inspiring story, or even the most generous act of service.
Only Christ can reconcile you to God.
So when you close this article, don't merely admire Rebekah.
Ask the Lord to make your heart more willing.
Ask Him to purify your motives.
Ask Him to teach you the difference between generous love and unhealthy self-neglect.
Ask Him to help you see the people you have been too busy to notice.
And above everything else, ask Him to keep your eyes fixed on Jesus.
Because the greatest miracle in Genesis 24 was not that a young woman worked hard enough to earn a wonderful future.
It was that God's providence was at work through ordinary people, ordinary decisions, and an ordinary encounter at a well.
And the greatest miracle offered to us in the Gospel is not that our kindness will make our dreams come true.
It is that Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died and rose again so that sinners could be forgiven and made new.
Maybe today, your assignment is not to change the whole world.
Maybe it is to tell the truth.
To forgive.
To repent.
To encourage someone.
To give without demanding applause.
To rest in Christ instead of trying to prove your worth.
To offer that ordinary cup of water in His name.
And maybe the person God is calling you to help will never be able to repay you.
Love them anyway.
Not because you know what you will receive.
But because you know the Savior who first loved you.
Rebekah never knew what waited beyond the well—but you can know the One whose grace is greater than everything you left behind.
